name: The Year I Started Secondary School
label: Journal for starting secondary school
title: The Year I Started Secondary School: a Year 7 journal for kids | Mazo Moon
description: A private, pressure-free journal for starting secondary school: first day, map of my school, calm toolkit and friendships. For Year 6 and Year 7. 110 pages.
card: A private place for a big new chapter.
h1: You don’t have to have it all figured out on day one
lead: A private, pressure-free journal for the big move to secondary school.
for: For Year 6 leavers getting ready over the summer
For Year 7s finding their feet in a new building with new people
For worriers, quiet ones and anyone who processes things on paper
hero: The Year I Started Secondary School cover

problem.h: New building, new people, new everything
p: Starting secondary school is a big deal. There are new routines, a timetable, getting lost between lessons, and working out where they fit, all at once.
A lot of that goes unsaid. Children often keep the worries in their head, where they feel bigger than they are.

approach.h: Somewhere to put it all down
p: This journal gives them a private place for the questions, the worries, the small wins and the moments worth remembering. They can fill it in before they start, during the first weeks, or whenever they need it.
There’s no right way to use it. Skip pages, come back later, write loads or a little. It’s theirs.

offer.h: A journal for the first year, at their pace
offer.p: Practical pages for finding their feet, and gentle ones for the feelings that come with it.
features: My first day, a map of my school to draw, and the rooms they need most.
Six things that help when it’s all a bit much, and a place they can go for a moment.
A “my people” circle for working out who feels close, old friends and new.

proof.p: Every page is about their experience, with no tests, no targets and nothing to get right.
note: I made this journal for the move that feels huge at eleven. I wanted it to say clearly, on the very first page, that nobody has to have it all figured out on day one.
It’s meant to be private, so it’s worth telling them that it’s theirs and nobody will read it unless they want them to.

items: A welcome page and a “this journal belongs to” name page
Finding my feet: my first day, map of my school and more
My calm toolkit and somewhere to go if I need a moment
People and friendships pages, including a “my people” circle
Mood faces to circle, lined pages and drawing spaces
110 pages in total, on cream paper

decision.h: One book for the whole first year
points: One paperback book, printed and posted by Amazon.
No subscription and nothing to download. Open it and start.
Amazon handles delivery and returns, just like anything else you buy there.

faq: When should I give it to them?
Any time from the end of Year 6 to the first term of Year 7. Some pages are for before they start, and lots are for the first weeks, but they can start whenever they like.
Is it only for nervous children?
No. Plenty of children are excited, and the journal keeps the good moments too. It just also has room for the wobbles.
Will they need help filling it in?
Most eleven-year-olds can use it on their own. It’s designed to be private, so it’s best to let them choose what to share.
Is it the same as a school planner?
No. There are no homework or timetable pages. It’s a journal about how they’re feeling and what they’re noticing.
Does it work for a new school in another year?
It’s written for starting secondary, but a child moving schools at any age would find most of the pages useful.

close.p: Give them somewhere to put it all, so they don’t have to carry it.
